points_json.example: A teacher gives one class extra tuition (the IV) and measures their exam marks (the DV) to see if tuition helped.
points_json.point: A variable is anything that can change or take different values — like age, temperature, or test score. In an experiment, the independent variable (IV) is what the researcher changes or controls. The dependent variable (DV) is what gets measured to see if the IV had an effect.

points_json.example: Testing three different study methods (levels of the IV) and comparing test scores (the DV).
points_json.point: The IV has levels — the different conditions being compared. A simple experiment has two levels, like treatment versus no treatment, but some have more. The DV must be measured carefully and consistently every time.

points_json.example: A researcher compares morning and evening classes, but the morning class also has a better teacher — teacher quality is the confound.
points_json.point: A confounding variable is an unwanted extra variable that changes along with the IV and ruins the experiment. If two things change at once, you cannot tell which one caused the result. This is the biggest enemy of good experiments.

points_json.example: Testing a memory drug where one group is younger on average — age confounds the result.
points_json.point: Participant variables like age, intelligence, or mood can confound results if groups are not equal. Situational variables like noise, room temperature, or time of day can also sneak in. Researchers must control or balance these.

points_json.example: Room noise affecting everyone's concentration equally is extraneous, but if only one group has noise, it becomes a confound.
points_json.point: Extraneous variables are any other variables that might affect the DV but are not the IV. Confounds are the dangerous type that vary systematically with the IV. Not every extraneous variable becomes a confound.

points_json.example: Defining aggression as the number of times a child hits a doll in 10 minutes.
points_json.point: Operational definitions state exactly how a variable will be measured or manipulated. Without them, research cannot be repeated or compared. Stress could mean heart rate, self-reported anxiety, or cortisol levels — the definition matters.

points_json.example: Testing all participants at the same time of day in the same quiet room.
points_json.point: Control variables are held constant on purpose so they cannot confound the study. Researchers list them in the method section. The more controlled the study, the cleaner the experiment — but too much control can make it artificial.

points_json.example: A researcher smiles more at the treatment group, accidentally encouraging them — an experimenter effect.
points_json.point: Demand characteristics and experimenter effects are sneaky confounds. Participants may guess the hypothesis and act to please the researcher. Experimenters may unconsciously treat groups differently. Double-blind procedures fix this.

summary: The building blocks of every experiment — what researchers change, what they measure, and the hidden variables that can ruin everything.
title: Variables: IV, DV and Confounds

points_json.example: Drinking coffee before an exam improves test scores.
points_json.point: A hypothesis is a clear, testable prediction about how two variables relate. It must be specific enough that data could prove it wrong. Studying helps is too vague; students who study 2 hours daily score higher is testable.

points_json.example: Cognitive dissonance theory explains why people justify bad decisions — and predicts dozens of specific behaviors.
points_json.point: A theory is a broad, well-supported explanation that organizes many findings. Theories explain WHY things happen, while hypotheses predict WHAT will happen. One theory can generate hundreds of hypotheses.

points_json.example: Null: The new drug has no effect on anxiety. Alternative: The new drug reduces anxiety.
points_json.point: The null hypothesis says there is no effect or no difference — it is the default position researchers try to reject. The alternative hypothesis says there IS an effect. Statistics test whether data is strong enough to reject the null.

points_json.example: Directional: Exercise reduces depression. Non-directional: Exercise affects depression.
points_json.point: Hypotheses can be directional, predicting the direction of change, or non-directional, just predicting a difference. Directional hypotheses are used when past research points one way. Non-directional ones are safer when unsure.

points_json.example: Listening to music while studying improves memory — this can be tested and potentially disproven.
points_json.point: A good hypothesis is falsifiable — it must be possible to prove it wrong. Invisible spirits affect mood cannot be tested, so it is not scientific. Falsifiability separates science from opinion.

points_json.example: Freud's catharsis theory was replaced when research showed venting anger increases aggression.
points_json.point: Theories are never proven — they are supported by evidence and can be revised or replaced. A strong theory explains a lot, makes accurate predictions, and stays simple. Weak theories get abandoned.

points_json.example: A diagram showing stress leading to poor sleep leading to low exam performance.
points_json.point: A conceptual model or framework maps how variables connect before testing. It guides which hypotheses to test and how. Models can be diagrams showing arrows between variables.

points_json.example: Noticing lonely students seem sadder leads to the hypothesis that loneliness predicts depression scores.
points_json.point: Hypotheses come from theories, past research, observations, or real-world problems. The best ones fill a clear gap in knowledge. A literature review finds what is already known before predicting something new.

summary: How science makes predictions — from testable guesses to grand explanations, and the logic that connects them.
title: Hypotheses and Theories

points_json.example: Randomly giving half the class a new textbook and comparing exam scores.
points_json.point: An experiment is the only method that can show cause and effect. The researcher manipulates the IV, controls everything else, and measures the DV. If groups differ only in the IV, the IV must have caused the difference.

points_json.example: Testing a sleep app — one group uses the app, the control group uses nothing.
points_json.point: Every experiment needs at least one experimental group that gets the treatment and ideally a control group that gets nothing or a placebo. Without a control group, you cannot tell if the treatment did anything.

points_json.example: Half the patients get the real pill, half get a sugar pill — neither knows which.
points_json.point: A placebo group receives a fake treatment to control for expectation effects. If the real treatment beats the placebo, the effect is genuine. Placebos can cause real improvements through belief alone.

points_json.example: After a stress induction, asking participants to rate their stress level to confirm it worked.
points_json.point: Manipulation checks confirm the IV actually worked as intended. Without them, a failed experiment might mean the treatment was too weak, not that the theory is wrong. Always verify the manipulation landed.

points_json.example: Testing persuasion with posters in a real shopping mall instead of a lab.
points_json.point: Experiments happen in labs with high control but artificial settings, or in the field with real settings but less control. Lab experiments maximize internal validity; field experiments maximize realism.

points_json.example: Testing a questionnaire on 10 students before giving it to 500.
points_json.point: Pilot studies are small trial runs before the real experiment. They catch confusing instructions, broken equipment, and weak manipulations. Skipping pilots wastes time and money.

points_json.example: Repeating a famous priming study in another country with new participants.
points_json.point: Replication means repeating a study to check the result holds. Direct replication repeats it exactly; conceptual replication tests the same idea differently. Science trusts findings only after replication.

points_json.example: Comparing students from two different schools that use different teaching methods.
points_json.point: Quasi-experiments look like experiments but lack random assignment — the groups already exist. They are useful when random assignment is impossible but cannot prove cause as strongly.

summary: The gold standard of research — how experiments prove cause and effect, and the essential parts every experiment needs.
title: Experimental Design Basics

points_json.example: Half the participants see happy faces, half see angry faces, then all rate their mood.
points_json.point: In a between-subjects design, each participant experiences only ONE condition. Different groups are compared. This is the most common experimental design in psychology.

points_json.example: Testing two website layouts with different users on each layout.
points_json.point: Between-subjects designs avoid order effects — participants cannot be influenced by conditions they never experienced. But they need more participants, and individual differences between groups can confound results. Random assignment fixes this.

points_json.example: Each participant takes a memory test sober and then again after coffee.
points_json.point: In a within-subjects design, EVERY participant experiences ALL conditions. Each person is compared to themselves. This controls individual differences perfectly.

points_json.example: Half the students do the easy test first, half do the hard test first — this is counterbalancing.
points_json.point: Within-subjects designs are powerful and need fewer participants, but suffer from order effects — practice, fatigue, or boredom from the first condition affects the second. Counterbalancing reduces this.

points_json.example: Testing two energy drinks back-to-back — the first drink's caffeine still affects the second test.
points_json.point: Carryover effects happen when one condition's influence bleeds into the next. A strong drug effect or learned strategy can contaminate later conditions. Washout periods, or breaks between conditions, help.

points_json.example: Pairing students by previous exam scores, then splitting each pair between two teaching methods.
points_json.point: Matched-subjects design is a middle ground — participants are paired on key traits like IQ, then one of each pair goes to each group. It balances groups without needing huge samples.

points_json.example: Men and women (between-subjects) each tested before and after therapy (within-subjects).
points_json.point: Mixed designs combine both — some variables are between-subjects, others within-subjects. This is common in real research and lets researchers answer richer questions.

points_json.example: You cannot unlearn a skill, so teaching-method studies must use between-subjects designs.
points_json.point: Choosing a design means trading off: between-subjects needs more people but is cleaner; within-subjects is efficient but risks order effects. If the treatment permanently changes participants, only between-subjects works.

summary: Two ways to run an experiment — different people in each group, or the same people in every condition. Each has strengths and traps.
title: Between vs Within Subjects Designs

points_json.example: Measuring hours of study and exam scores in 200 students to see if they move together.
points_json.point: Correlational research measures two variables to see if they move together — without manipulating anything. It shows relationships, not causes. It is perfect when experiments would be unethical or impossible.

points_json.example: Positive: exercise and fitness rise together. Negative: anxiety rises as sleep quality falls.
points_json.point: A positive correlation means both variables rise together. A negative correlation means one rises as the other falls. Zero correlation means no relationship at all.

points_json.example: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths correlate — but summer heat causes both.
points_json.point: Correlation does NOT prove causation — the most important rule in research methods. Two things can move together because a third variable causes both, or by pure coincidence. Never say causes from a correlation.

points_json.example: Do violent games cause aggression, or do aggressive kids choose violent games?
points_json.point: The third-variable problem means an unmeasured variable might explain the link. Directionality is also unknown — does A cause B, or B cause A? Only experiments untangle this.

points_json.example: Plotting sleep hours against alertness scores for 100 nurses to see the pattern.
points_json.point: Correlations are shown on scatterplots — each dot is one participant, and the pattern of dots reveals the relationship. Tight diagonal lines mean strong correlations; shapeless clouds mean weak ones.

points_json.example: Predicting job performance from intelligence, personality, and experience together.
points_json.point: Correlational studies can include many variables at once, unlike simple experiments. Multiple regression finds which variables best predict an outcome. This is how psychologists study complex real-life problems.

points_json.example: Measuring self-esteem and depression in teens, then again a year later, to hint at direction.
points_json.point: Cross-lagged panel designs measure two variables at two time points to hint at direction. If A at time 1 predicts B at time 2 better than the reverse, A likely influences B. Still not proof, but stronger evidence.

points_json.example: SAT scores predict college grades well, even though the SAT does not cause the grades.
points_json.point: Correlations are valuable for prediction even without causation. Insurance companies, admissions offices, and doctors use correlations to forecast outcomes daily. Prediction does not require understanding the cause.

summary: When two things move together — how researchers study relationships without experiments, and why correlation is not causation.
title: Correlational Research

points_json.example: A university surveying 2,000 students about mental health through an online form.
points_json.point: Surveys collect self-reported data from many people quickly and cheaply. They can reach thousands through online forms. They are the backbone of opinion, attitude, and market research.

points_json.example: An online happiness survey versus a face-to-face interview about trauma.
points_json.point: Questionnaires are written sets of questions; interviews are spoken. Questionnaires are cheaper and more private; interviews get deeper answers but cost more and risk interviewer bias.

points_json.example: Assisted suicide versus aid in dying gets very different support rates — wording matters.
points_json.point: Question wording shapes answers — leading questions push respondents toward an answer. Small wording changes create big result differences. Researchers must keep questions neutral.

points_json.example: Rating I feel stressed from 1 (never) to 5 (always) on a Likert scale.
points_json.point: Open questions give rich detail but are hard to analyze; closed questions are easy to analyze but limit answers. Likert scales from strongly agree to strongly disagree are the most popular format.

points_json.example: Asking about politics before asking about the economy changes the economy answer.
points_json.point: Order effects occur — earlier questions influence later answers. Randomizing question order or carefully sequencing questions reduces this bias.

points_json.example: Underreporting alcohol use on a survey to look responsible — social desirability bias.
points_json.point: Response biases distort surveys: social desirability means giving the good answer, acquiescence means agreeing with everything, extreme responding means only picking endpoints. Anonymous surveys help.

points_json.example: Emailing a survey three times to push responses from 30 percent to 65 percent.
points_json.point: Low response rates threaten surveys — if only 20 percent reply, they may differ from non-responders. Researchers send reminders, keep surveys short, and offer small incentives.

points_json.example: Testing a 50-item stress survey on 15 students before launching it widely.
points_json.point: Pilot testing a survey on a small group catches confusing questions before launch. Check that questions are clear, the survey is not too long, and the data looks sensible.

summary: Asking people questions at scale — how surveys work, the traps in question wording, and how to get honest answers.
title: Survey Methods

points_json.example: Studying HM, the famous amnesia patient, taught us how memory works.
points_json.point: A case study is an in-depth investigation of one person, group, or event. It uses interviews, tests, observations, and records to build a rich, detailed picture. It is ideal for rare conditions.

points_json.example: Phineas Gage's brain injury suggested the frontal lobe controls personality.
points_json.point: Case studies generate hypotheses for later testing — they are where many theories begin. Freud built psychoanalysis from case studies; Piaget studied his own children. They reveal what controlled studies might miss.

points_json.example: One patient's recovery does not prove a therapy works for everyone.
points_json.point: The biggest weakness is poor generalizability — one unusual person may not represent anyone else. Findings from a single case cannot be assumed true for the whole population.

points_json.example: A therapist's detailed notes on one client's progress over two years.
points_json.point: Case studies are rich in qualitative detail but often lack quantitative measurement. They describe but rarely test. Combining case studies with experiments gives both depth and proof.

points_json.example: A therapist who believes their method works may overlook the client's lack of progress.
points_json.point: Researcher bias is a real risk — the investigator may see what they expect. Without control groups or blinding, interpretations can be subjective. Multiple data sources strengthen conclusions.

points_json.example: Following a child with autism from diagnosis at age 3 to adulthood.
points_json.point: Longitudinal case studies follow one case over years, showing development and change. They are expensive but uniquely revealing — like the famous Genie language study.

points_json.example: Studying the few known patients with Capgras delusion, where each case is precious.
points_json.point: Case studies are essential for rare disorders where large samples are impossible. Much of neuropsychology was built on single brain-injury cases. Each rare case is a natural experiment.

points_json.example: Changing names, ages, and locations when publishing a therapy case.
points_json.point: Ethical care is critical — cases must be anonymized to protect identity. Famous cases like Little Albert would never be approved today. Informed consent is required whenever possible.

summary: Studying one person deeply — how single cases built psychology's greatest theories, and why they can't prove them.
title: Case Studies

points_json.example: Watching how children share toys in a playground without interfering.
points_json.point: Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting without interfering. The researcher is a fly on the wall. It captures real, spontaneous behavior that labs miss.

points_json.example: Observing parenting styles in family homes rather than in a laboratory.
points_json.point: This method has high ecological validity — findings apply to real life because they came from real life. Lab behavior can be artificial; natural behavior is genuine.

points_json.example: Two observers independently coding playground fights and comparing their notes.
points_json.point: Observer bias is the main threat — researchers may unconsciously record what they expect. Using clear coding schemes and multiple observers improves reliability. Inter-rater reliability should always be checked.

points_json.example: Workers performing better when they know a researcher is watching — the Hawthorne effect.
points_json.point: Reactivity happens if people know they are watched — they behave better or differently. Hidden observation avoids it but raises ethical questions. Unobtrusive measures help.

points_json.example: Recording every 30 seconds whether a student is on-task during class.
points_json.point: Coding systems turn messy behavior into data — like counting smiles per minute. Time sampling records at intervals; event sampling records each occurrence. Both make observation scientific.

points_json.example: Noticing bullied children sit alone, then experimentally testing an intervention.
points_json.point: Naturalistic observation describes but cannot explain cause — it shows WHAT happens, not WHY. It is often the first step, generating hypotheses for later experiments.

points_json.example: Jane Goodall spending months earning chimpanzees' trust before recording their tool use.
points_json.point: Famous examples shaped psychology: Goodall's chimpanzee observations, Piaget watching children play, studies of crowd behavior. These produced insights no lab could. Patience is the researcher's main tool.

points_json.example: Getting permission before observing behavior in a school classroom.
points_json.point: Ethics require care — observing in public places is usually fine, but private behavior needs consent. Debriefing and anonymity protect participants.

summary: Watching real behavior in the real world — the fly-on-the-wall method, its power, and its pitfalls.
title: Naturalistic Observation

points_json.example: Tracking 1,000 children from birth to age 30 to study life outcomes.
points_json.point: Longitudinal studies follow the SAME people over months or years, measuring them repeatedly. They show how individuals change and what predicts later outcomes. They are the gold standard for studying development.

points_json.example: The Dunedin study linking low self-control at age 5 to crime and health at age 30.
points_json.point: The huge strength of longitudinal research is seeing real change within people and establishing time order — what came first. No other design shows this as powerfully.

points_json.example: A 20-year study losing 40 percent of participants to moves and disinterest.
points_json.point: Longitudinal studies are expensive, slow, and lose participants over time — this is attrition. Those who drop out may differ from those who stay, biasing results. Researchers over-recruit to compensate.

points_json.example: Comparing memory scores of teenagers, adults, and seniors all tested in a single month.
points_json.point: Cross-sectional studies compare DIFFERENT groups at ONE point in time. They are fast and cheap, giving quick snapshots. Most developmental comparisons start here.

points_json.example: Older adults scoring lower on tech tasks may reflect less exposure, not cognitive decline — a cohort effect.
points_json.point: The cohort effect is cross-sectional's big flaw — groups differ not just in age but in generation. Today's 60-year-olds grew up without smartphones. This confound can mislead researchers.

points_json.example: Starting with 20-, 30-, and 40-year-olds and retesting all groups every 5 years.
points_json.point: Sequential designs combine both approaches — they follow several age groups over time. This separates age effects from cohort effects. It is the best of both worlds but complex and costly.

points_json.example: Studying aging needs longitudinal work; comparing current student attitudes needs only cross-sectional.
points_json.point: Choose longitudinal when studying change, causes over time, or development. Choose cross-sectional for quick comparisons, limited budgets, or when attrition would be severe.

points_json.example: IQ scores rising slightly on the second testing simply from familiarity with the test.
points_json.point: Practice effects threaten longitudinal studies — participants get better at tests just from repeating them. Using alternate test versions and long gaps between testing reduces this.

summary: Following the same people for years versus comparing different groups today — two ways to study change over time.
title: Longitudinal vs Cross-Sectional Studies

points_json.example: Population: all Pakistani university students. Sample: 300 students from 5 universities.
points_json.point: A population is everyone the researcher wants to learn about; a sample is the smaller group actually studied. Good research needs samples that represent the population.

points_json.example: Randomly selecting 500 voters from the electoral roll.
points_json.point: Random sampling gives every population member an equal chance of selection — like drawing names from a hat. It is the gold standard for representativeness, but it needs a full list of the population.

points_json.example: Sampling 50 percent men and 50 percent women to match the population proportions.
points_json.point: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups like age or gender, then randomly samples from each. This guarantees key groups are represented proportionally.

points_json.example: Randomly picking 10 schools and surveying all their students.
points_json.point: Cluster sampling randomly selects whole groups like schools or neighborhoods, then studies everyone inside. It is practical for large, spread-out populations.

points_json.example: Surveying every 20th customer entering a shopping mall.
points_json.point: Systematic sampling picks every nth person from a list. It is simple and spreads the sample evenly, but hidden patterns in the list can bias it.

points_json.example: Studying human memory using only 19-year-old undergraduates — the WEIRD problem.
points_json.point: Convenience sampling uses whoever is available. It is fast and cheap but badly biased. Most psychology research overuses it, studying Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic samples.

points_json.example: Finding rare-disease patients through patient support groups, each recruiting others.
points_json.point: Snowball sampling finds hard-to-reach people through referrals — each participant recruits others. It is essential for hidden populations but produces biased, connected samples.

points_json.example: Thirty participants per group is a common minimum for experiments.
points_json.point: Sample size matters — bigger samples give more reliable results and detect smaller effects. But a large biased sample just gives confident wrong answers. Power analysis calculates the needed size.

summary: Who gets studied — and why it matters. From gold-standard random sampling to the shortcuts researchers actually use.
title: Sampling Methods

points_json.example: Dealing participants into treatment or control groups like shuffling cards.
points_json.point: Random assignment means every participant has an equal chance of landing in any experimental group. It is different from random sampling, which is about choosing participants. Assignment is about placing them into groups.

points_json.example: Smarter students ending up equally in both groups purely by chance.
points_json.point: Its magic is balancing everything — known AND unknown differences — across groups. Age, intelligence, motivation, and even things the researcher never thought of get evenly spread. That is why experiments can claim cause and effect.

points_json.example: With 100 participants per group, ages and backgrounds even out nicely.
points_json.point: Random assignment only works with enough participants — with 6 people, chance can still create lopsided groups. Larger samples make the balancing more reliable. Researchers check that groups look similar afterward.

points_json.example: Comparing two existing classrooms — the better class might just have stronger students.
points_json.point: Without random assignment, you have a quasi-experiment — groups may differ from the start. Pre-existing differences become alternative explanations for any result. Conclusions must be cautious.

points_json.example: By chance, one group gets slightly more morning people in a single study.
points_json.point: Random assignment does not guarantee perfectly equal groups in any single study — it guarantees fairness of the PROCESS. Over many studies, the imbalances average out. One unlucky split can still happen.

points_json.example: Separating men and women first, then randomly assigning within each gender.
points_json.point: Blocking improves on pure randomness — participants are first grouped by an important trait, then randomly assigned within each block. This guarantees balance on that trait while keeping randomness.

points_json.example: Studying trauma effects must use naturally occurring groups — you cannot randomly assign trauma.
points_json.point: Random assignment is unethical or impossible sometimes — you cannot randomly assign child abuse, smoking, or gender. Then researchers use matching, statistical control, or quasi-experiments instead. Ethics always comes first.

points_json.example: A paper stating that a coin flip determined group membership.
points_json.point: Always report the assignment method in the method section so readers can judge the study. Participants were randomly assigned is a quality signal. If assignment was not random, say so honestly.

summary: The coin flip that makes experiments work — how random assignment creates fair groups and lets researchers claim cause and effect.
title: Random Assignment

points_json.example: A drug study with perfect controls has high internal validity — the drug clearly caused the change.
points_json.point: Internal validity asks: did the IV really cause the change in the DV, or did something else? It is about ruling out alternative explanations. High internal validity means the experiment was clean.

points_json.example: A happiness study conducted during a national tragedy — everyone's mood drops regardless of treatment.
points_json.point: History effects occur when outside events happen during the study and affect results. A news event, holiday, or campus crisis can change participants mid-study. Long studies are most vulnerable.

points_json.example: Children's vocabulary improving during a year-long study just from growing up.
points_json.point: Maturation is natural change over time — growing older, hungrier, tireder, or more bored. In long studies, participants change on their own. Control groups experiencing the same maturation cancel this out.

points_json.example: Scoring higher on the second IQ test just from knowing the test format.
points_json.point: Testing effects happen when taking a test once changes the next score — through practice, memory, or familiarity. Pre-tests can sensitize participants to the treatment.

points_json.example: An interviewer asking follow-up questions differently in the second group.
points_json.point: Instrumentation means the measuring tool changed — a rater gets stricter, a scale drifts, or observers get tired. If measurement shifts between groups, results are meaningless.

points_json.example: The lowest-scoring students improve on retest without any tutoring — regression to the mean.
points_json.point: Regression to the mean: extreme scores naturally move toward average on retesting. Selecting the worst performers guarantees improvement even with no treatment. This fools many into seeing effects that are not there.

points_json.example: Volunteers for a fitness program are already more motivated than non-volunteers.
points_json.point: Selection bias happens when groups differ from the start — the most dangerous threat in quasi-experiments. If the treatment group was already better, the effect is an illusion. Random assignment is the cure.

points_json.example: A tough therapy loses unhappy clients, making results look better than they really are.
points_json.point: Mortality, or attrition, is losing participants unevenly. If the weakest drop out of the treatment group, the remaining group looks artificially good. Researchers track dropout rates per group.

summary: Did the experiment really prove what it claims? The eight threats that can secretly ruin a study's conclusions.
title: Internal Validity

points_json.example: A memory technique that works in a quiet lab but fails in a noisy classroom.
points_json.point: External validity asks: do these results apply beyond this study — to other people, places, and times? It is about generalizability. A perfectly controlled lab study can still fail in the real world.

points_json.example: A parenting study on American mothers may not apply to Pakistani families.
points_json.point: Population validity is about WHO — do results generalize to other groups? Studies on Western undergraduates may not apply to older adults or other cultures. Diverse samples improve it.

points_json.example: Testing road rage in a driving simulator versus on real roads.
points_json.point: Ecological validity is about WHERE — does the setting resemble real life? Artificial labs lower it; natural settings raise it. Field experiments and naturalistic observation score high here.

points_json.example: Attention span studies from before social media may be outdated today.
points_json.point: Temporal validity is about WHEN — do results hold across time? Findings from the 1980s may not fit the smartphone era. Social norms, technology, and culture all shift.

points_json.example: A lab finds a persuasion trick; a field test checks if it works in actual shops.
points_json.point: There is a classic trade-off: tight lab control boosts internal validity but hurts external validity, while real-world studies reverse this. Good science needs both types of studies.

points_json.example: The marshmallow test replicated across cultures with varying results.
points_json.point: Replication across different populations, settings, and times builds external validity. One study proves little; twenty diverse studies prove a lot. Meta-analyses summarize this evidence.

points_json.example: Milgram's fake shocks felt real to participants — high psychological realism despite a lab setting.
points_json.point: Mundane realism, or superficial similarity to real life, matters less than psychological realism — engaging the same mental processes. A simple lab game can be highly valid if it triggers real emotions.

points_json.example: Stating honestly that results may not generalize beyond urban college students.
points_json.point: Researchers improve external validity with diverse samples, realistic tasks, and field settings. Describing the sample clearly lets readers judge generalizability. Honest limits sections help science.

summary: Do lab findings work in real life? Whether research results apply to other people, places, and times.
title: External Validity

points_json.example: Does an IQ test truly measure intelligence, or just test-taking skill?
points_json.point: Construct validity asks: are we really measuring what we claim to measure? A stress test that actually measures boredom has poor construct validity. It is the most theoretical type of validity.

points_json.example: A depression questionnaire asking about sadness has face validity — it looks right.
points_json.point: Face validity is the weakest form — does the test LOOK like it measures the right thing? It matters for participant cooperation but proves nothing scientifically. A test can look right and be wrong.

points_json.example: A driving test must cover parking, highways, and signals — not just parking.
points_json.point: Content validity means the test covers the FULL range of the concept — all important parts, nothing major missing. Experts judge whether items represent the whole domain. Crucial for achievement tests.

points_json.example: SAT scores predicting first-year college grades — predictive validity.
points_json.point: Criterion validity checks the test against a real-world standard. Concurrent validity compares with a current measure; predictive validity checks future outcomes like job success.

points_json.example: A new shyness scale should correlate with existing shyness scales but not with height.
points_json.point: Convergent validity means the test correlates with other measures of the SAME concept. Discriminant validity means it does NOT correlate with UNRELATED concepts. Both together prove the test measures what it should.

points_json.example: A math word-problem test accidentally measuring reading skill instead.
points_json.point: Threats include construct underrepresentation, measuring only one slice of the concept, and construct-irrelevant variance, where scores are affected by unrelated skills. Clean constructs avoid both.

points_json.example: Defining happiness as smiles per hour versus life satisfaction rating — very different constructs.
points_json.point: Operationalization is where construct validity is won or lost — the moment an abstract idea becomes a concrete measure. Poor operationalization dooms even brilliant theories.

points_json.example: An anxiety scale valid for adults may lack validity for children.
points_json.point: Building construct validity is ongoing — through factor analysis, correlations with related measures, and experiments. It is a property of how a test is USED, not of the test itself.

summary: Are we measuring what we think we're measuring? The deepest type of validity — and how researchers prove their tests are genuine.
title: Construct Validity

points_json.example: A bathroom scale showing different weights each minute is unreliable.
points_json.point: Reliability means consistency — getting similar results under similar conditions. Validity, or accuracy, is meaningless without reliability first. An unreliable measure cannot be trusted.

points_json.example: Giving an IQ test in January and again in March and expecting similar scores.
points_json.point: Test-retest reliability checks stability over time — same people, same test, two occasions. Scores should be similar if the trait is stable. Too long a gap allows real change; too short allows memory effects.

points_json.example: Two judges rating the same gymnastics performances should agree.
points_json.point: Inter-rater reliability checks agreement between different observers or judges. Two people rating the same behavior should reach similar scores. Essential for observations, interviews, and essay grading.

points_json.example: All 20 items of a depression scale pointing in the same direction.
points_json.point: Internal consistency checks whether items within ONE test agree with each other. Cronbach's alpha is the standard statistic — above 0.70 is acceptable, above 0.80 is good.

points_json.example: Comparing scores on questions 1 to 10 versus questions 11 to 20 of the same test.
points_json.point: Split-half reliability divides a test into two halves, like odd versus even items, and correlates them. It is a quick internal consistency check from a single administration.

points_json.example: Two different but equivalent versions of a university entrance exam.
points_json.point: Parallel forms reliability uses two different but equivalent versions of a test. It avoids memory effects of retesting with the same items. Creating truly parallel forms is difficult.

points_json.example: A broken clock is perfectly reliable — same wrong time twice a day — but never valid.
points_json.point: Reliability is necessary but NOT sufficient for validity. You can have reliability without validity, but never validity without reliability. A scale can consistently measure the wrong thing.

points_json.example: A 3-item quiz is less reliable than a 30-item one — longer tests are more consistent.
points_json.point: Factors hurting reliability include unclear questions, too few items, tired test-takers, and changing conditions. Longer tests, clear instructions, and standardized conditions improve it.

summary: Consistency is king — the four ways researchers check that their measurements give stable, dependable results.
title: Reliability Types

points_json.example: Describing the average salary in a company with a single typical number.
points_json.point: Central tendency describes the typical score in a dataset — the center point the data clusters around. The three measures are mean, median, and mode. Each tells a slightly different story.

points_json.example: Scores 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 give a mean of 4.
points_json.point: The mean is the arithmetic average — add all scores, divide by how many there are. It uses every score, making it sensitive and informative. But extreme outliers drag it away from the center.

points_json.example: Salaries of 30k, 32k, 35k, 38k, 500k give a median of 35k — the mean would mislead.
points_json.point: The median is the middle score when data is ordered from low to high. Half the scores are above it, half below. It ignores outliers, making it the best typical value for skewed data.

points_json.example: Shoe sizes 7, 8, 8, 9, 10 give a mode of 8 — the most frequent value.
points_json.point: The mode is the most frequent score — the value appearing most often. It is the only measure that works for categories like favorite color. A dataset can have two modes, called bimodal.

points_json.example: Mean house price versus median house price in a neighborhood with one mansion.
points_json.point: Outliers distort the mean but barely touch the median. With one billionaire in a room, the mean wealth skyrockets while the median stays normal. Always check for outliers first.

points_json.example: Perfectly symmetrical exam scores give identical mean, median, and mode.
points_json.point: In a normal bell-shaped distribution, mean, median, and mode are all equal at the center. In skewed distributions they split apart, and their positions reveal the skew direction.

points_json.example: Income data: the mean is higher than the median because the mean chases the tail.
points_json.point: In positively skewed data with a right tail like income, the order is mode, then median, then mean. In negatively skewed data it reverses. Remember: the mean chases the tail.

points_json.example: News reports giving both mean and median income for full transparency.
points_json.point: Report the median for skewed data like income and house prices, the mean for symmetrical data like heights, and the mode for categories. Good researchers often report both mean and median.

summary: Mean, median, mode — three ways to find the typical score, and how to pick the right one every time.
title: Central Tendency: Mean, Median, Mode

points_json.example: Two classes both average 70 percent, but one ranges 65 to 75 while the other ranges 30 to 100.
points_json.point: Variability describes how spread out scores are — clustered together or scattered widely? Two groups can share the same average but totally different spreads. Central tendency alone never tells the full story.

points_json.example: Scores from 40 to 95 give a range of 55.
points_json.point: The range is the simplest measure — highest score minus lowest score. It is quick but fragile, depending entirely on two extreme scores. One outlier can make it meaningless.

points_json.example: Test scores with a variance of 64, measured in squared marks.
points_json.point: Variance measures the average squared distance of scores from the mean. Squaring stops positive and negative distances from canceling out. Its units are squared, making it hard to interpret directly.

points_json.example: Mean of 70 with SD of 10 means most scores fall between 60 and 80.
points_json.point: Standard deviation is the square root of variance — bringing units back to normal. It tells the typical distance from the mean. About 68 percent of scores fall within one SD in normal data.

points_json.example: A class with SD of 5 is very consistent; SD of 20 means huge differences between students.
points_json.point: Small SD means scores cluster tightly around the mean — the group is consistent. Large SD means scores are spread out — the group is diverse. Comparing SDs reveals which group is more uniform.

points_json.example: An IQR of 60 to 80 means the middle half of students scored in that band.
points_json.point: The interquartile range covers the middle 50 percent of scores, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. Like the median, it resists outliers. Box plots display it visually.

points_json.example: Participants scored 75 percent on average with SD of 8.5.
points_json.point: Always report variability WITH central tendency — a mean without an SD is half the story. Together they describe both the center and the spread. This is standard in every research paper.

points_json.example: Testing everyone in the same quiet room reduces random variation between scores.
points_json.point: Variability affects what statistics can detect — with huge spread, real differences hide in the noise. Reducing unwanted variability through control makes effects easier to find.

summary: How spread out are the scores? Range, variance, and standard deviation — the measures that complete the picture.
title: Variability: Range, Variance, SD

points_json.example: The heights of adult women cluster around the average, with few very short or very tall.
points_json.point: The normal distribution is the famous bell curve — symmetrical, with most scores in the middle and fewer at the extremes. Heights, IQ scores, and measurement errors often follow it.

points_json.example: IQ has a mean of 100, so most people score near 100.
points_json.point: In a perfect normal distribution, the mean, median, and mode are identical at the center peak. The curve is symmetrical: the left mirrors the right.

points_json.example: An IQ of 130, two SDs above 100, is in the top 2.5 percent of people.
points_json.point: The 68-95-99.7 rule: 68 percent of scores fall within 1 SD of the mean, 95 percent within 2 SDs, 99.7 percent within 3 SDs. Beyond 2 SDs is genuinely rare.

points_json.example: A t-test on 200 participants tolerates slight skew in the data.
points_json.point: Many statistical tests assume normality — they work best when data is roughly bell-shaped. With large samples, minor violations are okay. Researchers check with histograms.

points_json.example: House prices are positively skewed — most are modest, a few are enormous.
points_json.point: Skewed distributions lean one way: positive skew has a long right tail like income; negative skew has a long left tail like an easy exam. Skew changes which average to trust.

points_json.example: Reaction times often form a peaked, right-skewed curve rather than a perfect bell.
points_json.point: Kurtosis describes peakedness — tall narrow peaks versus flat wide ones. It matters less often but affects some advanced tests. Most researchers just eyeball the shape.

points_json.example: The average of 100 dice rolls forms a bell curve, though single rolls are flat.
points_json.point: The central limit theorem is statistics' superpower: averages of large samples become normally distributed EVEN IF the raw data is not. This is why normal-based tests work so widely.

points_json.example: Taking the log of income data to make its skewed shape bell-like.
points_json.point: Real data is never perfectly normal — and that is fine. Approximately normal is enough for most purposes. Transformations like logarithms can fix strong skew. Always plot your data first.

summary: The bell curve that rules statistics — why so much data piles up in the middle, and the famous 68-95-99.7 rule.
title: Normal Distribution

points_json.example: Scoring 130 on an IQ test with mean 100 and SD 15 gives a z-score of +2.
points_json.point: A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a score sits above or below the mean. It is a universal translator converting any score into standard units. Plus 1 means one SD above average.

points_json.example: A z of +1.5 in math versus +0.5 in English shows relatively stronger math performance.
points_json.point: Z-scores let you compare apples and oranges — scores from completely different tests. The higher z-score shows the stronger relative performance, whatever the original scales were.

points_json.example: Heights, weights, and test scores all become comparable once converted to z-scores.
points_json.point: The z-distribution always has a mean of 0 and SD of 1, no matter the original data. Every normal distribution maps onto the same standard curve through this transformation.

points_json.example: A z-score of +2.5 puts you above 99 percent of people.
points_json.point: Z-scores reveal how unusual a score is: beyond plus or minus 2 is uncommon, beyond plus or minus 3 is extremely rare. Researchers use these cutoffs to flag outliers.

points_json.example: Score 85, mean 70, SD 10: subtract the mean and divide by SD to get z = +1.5.
points_json.point: To compute one: subtract the mean from the score, then divide by the standard deviation. Just two steps — no heavy math needed. Most calculators do it instantly.

points_json.example: A z of 0 is the 50th percentile; z of +1 is about the 84th percentile.
points_json.point: Percentiles connect to z-scores through conversion tables. This is how standardized test reports translate scores into rankings everyone understands.

points_json.example: A t-test is essentially comparing z-like scores between two groups.
points_json.point: Z-scores are the building blocks of many statistics — correlation, regression, and hypothesis tests all use them behind the scenes. They are the common currency of inferential statistics.

points_json.example: A z of +3 in depression scores is alarming but does not explain WHY the depression exists.
points_json.point: Watch out: z-scores assume roughly normal data — with heavily skewed data they mislead. A z-score describes a score's position, never its cause.

summary: One number that lets you compare any scores — how z-scores turn different tests into the same universal language.
title: Z-Scores Explained Simply

points_json.example: An r of 0.70 between study hours and grades shows a strong positive link.
points_json.point: A correlation coefficient is a single number, r, summarizing how strongly two variables relate — from minus 1 to plus 1. It is the standard language for relationships in psychology.

points_json.example: An r of −0.60 between stress and sleep quality: as stress rises, sleep falls.
points_json.point: The sign shows direction: positive r means both rise together; negative r means one rises as the other falls. The size shows strength: near 0 is weak, near plus or minus 1 is strong.

points_json.example: An r of 0.25 between therapy and recovery can be clinically meaningful.
points_json.point: Rough guide: 0.10 is small, 0.30 is medium, 0.50-plus is large. In psychology, even 0.30 can matter enormously for real lives. Context decides importance, not just the number.

points_json.example: Pearson for height and weight; Spearman for ranked movie preferences.
points_json.point: Pearson's r is most common — for two continuous variables with a linear relationship. Spearman's rho handles ranked data. Point-biserial works when one variable is yes-or-no. Match the coefficient to the data.

points_json.example: An r of 0.40 means 16 percent of grade differences are explained by study hours.
points_json.point: Squaring r gives r-squared — the percentage of variation in one variable explained by the other. An r of 0.50 means 25 percent shared variance. This is often more meaningful than r itself.

points_json.example: Moderate stress helps performance but too little or too much hurts — r near 0 despite a real link.
points_json.point: Correlation needs linearity — it misses curved relationships. A U-shaped link can show r near 0 despite a strong pattern. Always plot the scatterplot first.

points_json.example: The SAT-grade correlation looks smaller within Harvard than nationally — restricted range.
points_json.point: Restricted range shrinks correlations — studying only top students makes the study-grade link look weak. Outliers can also inflate or deflate r dramatically. Check your data's spread.

points_json.example: An r of 0.80 between ice cream sales and drownings — summer heat explains both.
points_json.point: Remember the mantra: correlation does not imply causation. A strong r only shows variables move together. Third variables, reverse causation, or coincidence may explain it.

summary: The number that measures relationships — how to read r values, what counts as strong, and the traps to avoid.
title: Correlation Coefficients

points_json.example: A p of 0.01 means such results would happen only 1 percent of the time by pure chance.
points_json.point: A p-value answers: if there were really no effect, how surprising would my data be? Small p means the data would be very surprising with no effect — so an effect probably exists. It is NOT the probability that the hypothesis is true.

points_json.example: A drug trial with p = 0.03 is declared statistically significant.
points_json.point: The magic cutoff is 0.05 — below it, results are called statistically significant. This is just a convention from the 1920s, not a law of nature. p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 are practically identical.

points_json.example: A pill improving mood by 0.1 percent with p = 0.001 — significant but useless.
points_json.point: Significant means statistically surprising, NOT important. A tiny, meaningless effect can be significant with a huge sample. Always ask about the effect SIZE too, not just the p-value.

points_json.example: Many findings with p below 0.05 failed when other labs tried to replicate them.
points_json.point: P-values do NOT tell you the probability your hypothesis is true, or that results will replicate. p = 0.04 does not mean a 96 percent chance the effect is real. This misunderstanding fueled the replication crisis.

points_json.example: Testing 20 outcomes and publishing only the one that worked — p-hacking.
points_json.point: P-hacking is torturing data until p drops below 0.05 — trying many analyses and reporting only the winner. It produces false positives that pollute science. Pre-registering analyses prevents it.

points_json.example: A therapy that works may show p = 0.20 in a tiny underpowered study.
points_json.point: Non-significant, p above 0.05, does NOT prove no effect — it just means the evidence was too weak. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Small samples often miss real effects.

points_json.example: The improvement was 5 points, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 1 to 9.
points_json.point: Confidence intervals are better companions — they show the range of plausible values for the effect. A narrow interval near zero means a tiny effect; a wide one means uncertainty. Report both p and intervals.

points_json.example: The famous power posing effect failed to replicate despite an impressive original p-value.
points_json.point: The replication crisis taught psychology humility — many classic findings with p below 0.05 did not replicate. Now researchers demand bigger samples, pre-registration, and effect sizes. One p-value never settles anything.

summary: The most misunderstood number in science — what p-values really mean, and why significant doesn't mean important.
title: P-Values Explained Simply

points_json.example: Do coffee drinkers score differently on alertness than non-drinkers?
points_json.point: A t-test compares the averages of TWO groups to see if they truly differ or if the gap is just chance. It is the most-used test in psychology. Two groups and one measurement means think t-test.

points_json.example: Comparing exam scores of students who used flashcards versus those who did not.
points_json.point: The independent-samples t-test compares two SEPARATE groups, like treatment versus control. It asks whether their means differ more than random variation would allow. Random assignment makes this valid.

points_json.example: Measuring anxiety before and after therapy for each individual patient.
points_json.point: The paired-samples t-test compares the SAME people twice — before and after, or in two conditions. Each person is their own control, making it more powerful. It analyzes differences within each pair.

points_json.example: Testing whether a school's average IQ differs from the national average of 100.
points_json.point: The one-sample t-test compares ONE group against a known value or benchmark. It is less common but useful when a standard exists to compare against.

points_json.example: The therapy group averaged 12, controls averaged 18, with t = 3.2 and p = 0.002.
points_json.point: The t-test produces a t-value, where bigger means a bigger difference relative to variation, plus a p-value. If p is below 0.05, the difference is statistically significant. Report means, t, and p together.

points_json.example: Comparing incomes, which are heavily skewed, might need a Mann-Whitney test instead.
points_json.point: Assumptions matter: roughly normal data, and similar variability in both groups for independent tests. With decent sample sizes, t-tests tolerate violations. Very skewed data may need non-parametric alternatives.

points_json.example: A d of 0.9 means a large, meaningful gap between the two groups.
points_json.point: A significant t-test does not show HOW BIG the difference is — that is the effect size, Cohen's d. Values of 0.2 are small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Big samples can make tiny differences significant.

points_json.example: Testing 5 groups with 10 separate t-tests instead of one ANOVA inflates false positives.
points_json.point: Common mistakes: using the independent t-test on paired data or vice versa, running many t-tests instead of ANOVA, and ignoring assumptions. Always match the test to the design.

summary: Comparing two averages the right way — the three types of t-tests and when to use each one.
title: T-Tests Explained Simply

points_json.example: Comparing test scores across four different teaching methods at once.
points_json.point: ANOVA, or Analysis of Variance, compares averages across THREE OR MORE groups at once. Running many t-tests instead would inflate false alarms — ANOVA controls this with a single test.

points_json.example: An F of 8.5 means between-group differences dwarf the random noise inside groups.
points_json.point: The F-ratio is ANOVA's core: variation BETWEEN groups divided by variation WITHIN groups. Big differences between groups relative to noise inside groups gives a large F and a significant result.

points_json.example: ANOVA says the four diets differ; follow-up tests reveal diet C beats the rest.
points_json.point: A significant ANOVA only says at least one group differs — not WHICH ones. Post-hoc tests like Tukey's then compare pairs while controlling error. Never skip this step.

points_json.example: A teaching method helps boys but not girls — that interaction is the real discovery.
points_json.point: One-way ANOVA has one independent variable. Two-way factorial ANOVA has two and can detect interactions — when one variable's effect depends on the other. Interactions are often the most interesting finding.

points_json.example: Testing each participant under quiet, noisy, and music conditions.
points_json.point: Repeated-measures ANOVA is for within-subjects designs — the same people in all conditions. It is more powerful because individual differences are removed from the error.

points_json.example: Groups of 30 each handle mild skew in the data just fine.
points_json.point: ANOVA assumes roughly normal data, similar variances across groups, and independent observations. Moderate violations are tolerable with equal group sizes. Levene's test checks the variance assumption.

points_json.example: An eta-squared of 0.14 means teaching method explains 14 percent of score differences.
points_json.point: Effect size for ANOVA is eta-squared — the proportion of total variation explained by the groups. Like r-squared, it shows practical importance beyond the p-value. Always report it.

points_json.example: Comparing satisfaction ratings across three stores with the Kruskal-Wallis test.
points_json.point: When ANOVA assumptions badly fail, use non-parametric alternatives: Kruskal-Wallis instead of one-way ANOVA, Friedman instead of repeated-measures. These use ranks instead of raw scores.

summary: Comparing three or more groups at once — how ANOVA works, what the F-ratio means, and finding which groups differ.
title: ANOVA Basics

points_json.example: Do more students prefer morning or evening classes? Count and compare.
points_json.point: The chi-square test works with CATEGORIES, not numbers — like yes or no, pass or fail. It compares what you OBSERVED against what you would EXPECT by chance. It is the go-to test for frequency data.

points_json.example: Testing whether a die is fair — are all six faces equally likely?
points_json.point: The goodness-of-fit version tests ONE categorical variable against expected proportions. Are the observed counts surprisingly different from an even split or any expected pattern?

points_json.example: Is gender related to preferred study method — groups versus studying alone?
points_json.point: The test of independence checks whether TWO categorical variables are related. It builds a contingency table and asks if the patterns differ from chance. This is the most common chi-square use.

points_json.example: Expecting a 50-50 split but observing 70-30 raises suspicion.
points_json.point: Expected frequencies are the key calculation — the counts you would see if there were no relationship. The test sums how far observed counts deviate from these. Bigger deviations give bigger chi-square and smaller p.

points_json.example: A 2x2 table with expected counts of 2 needs Fisher's exact test instead.
points_json.point: Each cell needs enough data — expected frequencies should be at least 5 in most cells. Tiny samples make chi-square unreliable. Always check this assumption before trusting results.

points_json.example: A significant chi-square with Cramer's V of 0.15 means a real but weak link.
points_json.point: A significant chi-square says variables are related — but NOT how strongly. Cramer's V measures the strength, like a correlation for categories. Always report it alongside.

points_json.example: Chi-square shows smoking relates to gender but not which causes which.
points_json.point: Chi-square cannot show direction or cause — only that categories associate. It also cannot handle means or continuous data. Match the test to the data type.

points_json.example: Do dropout rates differ across three therapy programs? Count and test.
points_json.point: Common uses: testing if therapy outcomes differ by treatment type, if diagnoses distribute equally across groups, or if survey responses differ by demographic. Any counts-in-categories question fits.

summary: Statistics for categories — how chi-square tests whether counts differ from chance, with yes/no style data.
title: Chi-Square Test Basics

points_json.example: Predicting exam scores from hours studied with a best-fitting line.
points_json.point: Regression predicts one variable FROM another — going beyond correlation's they relate to given X, what is Y? It draws the best-fitting line through scatterplot data. Prediction is its superpower.

points_json.example: Each extra study hour predicts 3 more exam marks.
points_json.point: Simple regression uses ONE predictor in the equation Y = a + bX. The slope shows how much Y changes per unit of X; the intercept is Y when X is zero. This line minimizes prediction errors.

points_json.example: Predicting salary from education, experience, and city together.
points_json.point: Multiple regression uses SEVERAL predictors at once — like predicting job performance from IQ, experience, AND personality. It reveals each predictor's unique contribution while controlling the others.

points_json.example: Study habits explaining 40 percent of grade differences — R-squared of 0.40.
points_json.point: R-squared shows the percentage of Y's variation explained by the predictors. Higher is better, but psychology rarely exceeds 0.50 — human behavior is complex. Adjusted R-squared penalizes useless predictors.

points_json.example: Motivation with beta 0.45 matters more than sleep with beta 0.20 for grades.
points_json.point: Beta weights, or standardized coefficients, compare predictors' relative importance on the same scale. The biggest beta matters most. Unstandardized weights give real-unit predictions.

points_json.example: The 10th study hour helps less than the 1st — diminishing returns curve the line.
points_json.point: Regression assumes linear relationships and roughly normal prediction errors. Violations distort results. Always plot residuals to check. Curved relationships need different models.

points_json.example: Ice cream sales predict drownings but do not cause them.
points_json.point: Correlation is not causation applies here too — regression cannot prove X causes Y. It only models association. A third variable may drive both. Experiments or strong theory are needed for causal claims.

points_json.example: A 20-predictor model built on 40 people is mostly fiction — overfitting.
points_json.point: Overfitting happens when too many predictors chase noise in small samples — the model fits the sample perfectly but fails on new data. Keep predictors few relative to sample size. Simpler models generalize better.

summary: Predicting the future from data — how regression draws the line of best fit and what R-squared really tells you.
title: Regression Basics

points_json.example: A drug beating placebo by 1 percent versus by 40 percent — same significance, very different importance.
points_json.point: Effect size answers HOW BIG is the difference — the question p-values cannot answer. A tiny effect can be significant with huge samples; a huge effect can miss significance in tiny samples.

points_json.example: A d of 1.0 means groups differ by a full standard deviation — a big deal.
points_json.point: Cohen's d measures standardized difference between two means: 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. It puts effects on a universal scale comparable across all studies.

points_json.example: An r of 0.15 for a cheap, harmless intervention given to millions still matters.
points_json.point: Correlation r IS an effect size: 0.10 small, 0.30 medium, 0.50 large. Squaring it gives variance explained. Context can make statistically small effects vitally important.

points_json.example: An eta-squared of 0.20 means the treatment explains 20 percent of outcome differences.
points_json.point: Eta-squared for ANOVA and R-squared for regression show proportion of variance explained — 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large. They answer what percentage of differences this explains.

points_json.example: Therapy doubles the odds of recovery — an odds ratio of 2.0.
points_json.point: Odds ratios and risk ratios suit yes-or-no outcomes. They are intuitive for medical and clinical research. Convert them to plain language so readers grasp the meaning.

points_json.example: A d of 0.60 with a confidence interval from 0.40 to 0.80 is a solid estimate.
points_json.point: Confidence intervals around effect sizes show precision — narrow intervals mean confident estimates. Report intervals, not just point values, so readers see the uncertainty.

points_json.example: An expensive therapy with d of 0.1 may simply not be worth the cost.
points_json.point: Practical significance asks: does this effect matter in real life? A statistically significant 2-point IQ gain changes nothing; a 15-point gain changes lives. Cost, risk, and context decide.

points_json.example: Fifty studies' d values averaged together reveal therapy's true overall benefit.
points_json.point: The replication crisis pushed effect sizes center-stage — journals now require them. Meta-analyses combine effect sizes across studies. Science moved from is there an effect to how big is it.

summary: How big is the difference, really? Why effect sizes matter more than p-values — and how to read them.
title: Effect Sizes

points_json.example: Understanding what grief feels like for widows — in their own words.
points_json.point: Qualitative research explores MEANING, not numbers — how people experience and interpret their world. It uses words, stories, and observations. It answers how and why, not how many.

points_json.example: Semi-structured interviews about students' exam anxiety — guided but flexible.
points_json.point: Interviews are the backbone: structured uses fixed questions, semi-structured is guided but flexible and most popular, unstructured is free conversation. Good interviewing means listening more than talking.

points_json.example: A group discussion revealing attitudes toward campus counseling that individuals would not voice alone.
points_json.point: Focus groups gather 6 to 10 people to discuss a topic — interactions spark ideas individuals would not raise alone. A skilled moderator keeps discussion balanced. They are fast and rich.

points_json.example: Finding themes of isolation and hope across twenty depression narratives.
points_json.point: Thematic analysis finds patterns or themes across qualitative data — coding transcripts, grouping codes, refining themes. It is the most widely used qualitative method. Rigor comes from systematic coding.

points_json.example: Developing a theory of how teens cope with bullying, built from their own accounts.
points_json.point: Grounded theory BUILDS theory from data — collecting and analyzing simultaneously until no new ideas emerge. It is ideal when little is known. Theory emerges from participants' words.

points_json.example: Studying what it is LIKE to live with postpartum depression — deep and personal.
points_json.point: Phenomenology studies lived experience in depth. Small samples, deep interviews, rich description. It honors subjective reality and captures what numbers cannot.

points_json.example: Living in a village for a year to truly understand child-rearing practices.
points_json.point: Ethnography immerses the researcher in a culture or group for extended time — observing, participating, learning from inside. It reveals what surveys miss but demands patience.

points_json.example: Sharing the found themes with interviewees to confirm the interpretation is accurate.
points_json.point: Quality in qualitative research means credibility, transferability, and reflexivity — the researcher examining their own biases. Member checking, where participants review findings, strengthens trust.

summary: Research with words instead of numbers — interviews, focus groups, and how scientists study human meaning rigorously.
title: Qualitative Research Methods

points_json.example: Combining 100 therapy studies to find therapy's true overall effectiveness.
points_json.point: A meta-analysis statistically COMBINES many studies on one question into a single answer. Instead of one study's verdict, you get the weighted average of dozens. It sits at the top of the evidence pyramid.

points_json.example: Fifty studies averaging to d of 0.70 for CBT treating anxiety.
points_json.point: Effect sizes are the currency — each study contributes its d or r, weighted by sample size so bigger studies count more. The pooled effect is far more reliable than any single study.

points_json.example: A diamond at d of 0.5 not touching zero means a solid, real effect.
points_json.point: Forest plots display results visually — each study is a dot with a confidence interval line, and the diamond at the bottom is the combined effect. If the diamond clears zero, the effect is real.

points_json.example: Therapy works better for adults than children — age moderates the effect.
points_json.point: Heterogeneity measures how much studies DISAGREE. High heterogeneity means effects vary widely. Moderator analysis then asks WHY — different populations or methods? Variation is informative.

points_json.example: A funnel plot missing small negative studies signals publication bias.
points_json.point: Publication bias is meta-analysis's enemy — positive studies get published, negative ones vanish. Funnel plots detect this: asymmetry suggests missing studies. Statistical methods adjust the estimates.

points_json.example: Only randomized trials from 2000 to 2024 with adult samples — set before searching.
points_json.point: Inclusion criteria decide which studies count — and must be set BEFORE searching. Clear rules prevent cherry-picking favorable studies. PRISMA guidelines standardize the reporting.

points_json.example: The famous Mozart effect shrinking to near-zero when all studies were combined.
points_json.point: Meta-analyses can overturn established findings — single famous studies often shrink when combined with replications. They are science's self-correction engine.

points_json.example: A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it includes — garbage in, garbage out.
points_json.point: Limitations exist: combining flawed studies gives flawed answers, and mixing very different studies can mislead. Quality assessment of included studies is essential.

summary: Combining dozens of studies into one answer — how meta-analysis settles scientific debates and spots hidden biases.
title: Meta-Analysis

points_json.example: A consent form explaining a 30-minute memory experiment before anyone agrees.
points_json.point: Informed consent means participants understand what they are joining — purpose, procedures, risks, and their right to quit anytime — BEFORE agreeing. It must be fully voluntary, without pressure.

points_json.example: Telling participants a test measures reaction time when it really measures prejudice.
points_json.point: Deception is sometimes necessary but tightly restricted — it must be justified, cause no serious harm, and be followed by full debriefing. Ethics boards scrutinize every deception study.

points_json.example: Explaining the conformity study afterward and why the group gave wrong answers on purpose.
points_json.point: Debriefing happens after the study — explaining the true purpose, answering questions, and undoing negative effects. It is mandatory when deception was used.

points_json.example: Storing surveys with ID numbers, never with participants' names.
points_json.point: Confidentiality protects identities — data is coded, names removed, and results reported in groups. Anonymity, where not even the researcher knows who said what, is even stronger.

points_json.example: A participant leaving a stressful task halfway with full credit still intact.
points_json.point: The right to withdraw means participants can quit anytime without penalty — even mid-experiment, even after consenting. Grades or pay cannot depend on finishing.

points_json.example: Getting both parental consent AND the child's own agreement for a study.
points_json.point: Vulnerable populations — children, prisoners, the mentally ill — need extra protection, often guardian consent plus the person's assent. Power differences demand special care.

points_json.example: A board rejecting a study that withholds effective treatment from its control group.
points_json.point: Institutional Review Boards approve all human research before it starts. They weigh risks against benefits and can demand changes or reject studies entirely. No approval means no research.

points_json.example: The Tuskegee study ran 40 years without treating participants — why modern ethics codes exist.
points_json.point: Infamous violations teach why ethics matter: Tuskegee, Milgram's extreme stress, Little Albert. Modern codes like the Nuremberg Code and APA ethics exist because of these failures.

summary: The moral backbone of science — consent, deception, debriefing, and the scandals that made ethics rules necessary.
title: Research Ethics in Depth

points_json.example: Screening 20 papers by reading only their abstracts in 30 minutes.
points_json.point: Read strategically, not front-to-back: start with the ABSTRACT, then jump to the DISCUSSION, then RESULTS, and read the METHOD only if needed. This approach saves hours.

points_json.example: Finding the gap: no studies have tested this intervention in teenagers.
points_json.point: The introduction sets up the problem — what is known, what is missing, and the current hypotheses. Skim for the research question and predictions.

points_json.example: Noticing a study used only 15 participants — an immediate red flag.
points_json.point: The method section lets you judge quality — who participated, what was done, and how variables were measured. Ask: was there random assignment? A control group? Valid measures?

points_json.example: A bar graph showing the therapy group clearly outperforming the controls.
points_json.point: Results report statistics, not stories — means, p-values, effect sizes. Focus on the tables and figures; they summarize everything. Check whether effects are statistically AND practically significant.

points_json.example: Authors honestly admitting their student sample limits generalizability.
points_json.point: The discussion interprets results — do they support the hypotheses? Good papers admit limitations honestly and suggest next steps. Be skeptical of overclaiming.

points_json.example: A correlation study boldly claiming proof that games cause violence.
points_json.point: Evaluate critically: Is the sample adequate? Are measures valid? Do conclusions match the data? Could confounds explain it? Has it been replicated? One study never proves anything.

points_json.example: A 2010 paper cited 2,000 times is influential — for better or worse.
points_json.point: Check references and citations — highly cited papers in good journals carry more weight. But citation counts can also reflect controversy. See who cited it and what they said.

points_json.example: A one-paragraph summary card for every paper you read, in your own words.
points_json.point: Take notes: research question, method, key finding, limitation, and your critique. Reading 5 papers deeply beats skimming 50. Build a personal database of summaries.

summary: Don't read papers front-to-back — the smart strategy for understanding research quickly and judging it critically.
title: How to Read a Research Paper
